newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: ARGENTINE COMPANIES STILL WARY OF GOING PUBLIC.
newsitem.headline: ARGENTINE COMPANIES STILL WARY OF GOING PUBLIC.

text.p: Argentine companies are still reluctant to be listed on the Buenos Aires stock exchange, according to a study carried out by the bourse's think tank Capital Markets Institute (IAMC).
The survey, published Monday in the local daily El Cronista, shows the main deterrents are financial disclosure requirements and greater administrative costs incurred by listed companies.
Seventy-seven percent of the 410 respondents said they had never considered the possibility of trading on the bourse. Only nine percent had considered it recently.
Thirty-eight percent said the main disadvantage to being publicly traded are the disclosure rules, although 87 percent were not sure exactly what those requirements are.
Thirty percent blamed higher paperwork costs, while 12 percent feared having unknown partners, and nine percent losing control of the company.

El Cronista noted the number of listed companies had shrunk to 203 today from 552 in 1960, while the ratio between market capitalization and GDP was 18.5 percent in Buenos Aires against 30.1 percent in Sao Paulo, 32.4 percent in Mexico City and 103.2 percent in Santiago de Chile.
The survey also showed companies preferred to obtain financing from suppliers.
"This shows there is a short-term financing strategy," IAMC, which "is more a byproduct of the companies' commercial activities than an explicit financing plan."
Only two percent of small firms, eight percent of medium-sized firms and three percent of large companies said they did not want to trade on the bolsa because it was not transparent enough.
